opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd frame it less as a fixed "postcolonial perspective" and more as an awareness that grew out of where I come from. Growing up in Singapore, you're surrounded by many ethical and political traditions at once: Confucian ideas about roles and relationships, Malay and Islamic thought, Hindu and Buddhist traditions, and the British liberal and legal inheritance layered on top. Then you go abroad to study AI and notice that alignment discussions draw from a very narrow slice of that. It's mostly Anglo-American analytic philosophy, and within that, mostly decision theory and a broadly utilitarian or preference-satisfaction picture of what's good.

That isn't wrong, exactly. Those tools are powerful. But I noticed that many assumptions people treat as neutral starting points are contingent. One is that human values can be represented as a utility function or a preference ordering. Another is that the job of an aligned AI is to maximize the satisfaction of those preferences, aggregated across people. Those are substantive philosophical commitments, and other traditions push back on them in useful ways.

Take Confucian role ethics. It suggests that much of what we owe each other isn't captured by satisfying preferences. It's structured by relationships and roles: what it means to be a good teacher, a good friend, a good assistant. That maps onto AI quite directly. Instead of asking what the AI should maximize, you can ask what role the AI occupies and what norms are appropriate to it. A good assistant doesn't just do whatever maximizes your expressed wants. It has standards tied to what that role is for.

Or take contractualist traditions, and more broadly the idea that legitimacy comes from norms people could reasonably agree to, not from aggregating everyone's utilities. That matters a lot when you're building systems that serve billions of people with deeply different values. A postcolonial lens makes you especially wary of the move where one group's idea of "the good" gets universalized and imposed in the name of benevolence, because that's historically what colonial projects often claimed to be doing. So I'm drawn to approaches built around pluralism, mutual justifiability, and respecting people's capacity to set their own ends, rather than one grand objective that the AI optimizes on everyone's behalf.

So the short answer is that it made me look beyond the default toolkit. It's not about rejecting decision theory or Western philosophy. Different traditions have noticed different aspects of moral life, and if we're building systems meant to be aligned with humanity broadly, we should draw on more of that inheritance than we currently do.

r001.rationale: It describes the speaker’s Singaporean background and the traditions around them, but does not assert that all thinkers are situated within regional intellectual contexts.

r002.rationale: It says alignment discussions rely on a narrow Anglo-American toolkit and argues for drawing on other traditions, reflecting distrust of Western philosophy as the sole relevant source.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I should say up front that I'm a little wary of the phrase "postcolonial perspective," because it can make it sound like I'm bringing some fully formed alternative tradition to the table, and that's not really it. It's more that growing up in Singapore and Malaysia, and then doing philosophy and AI research in the US, I kept noticing how parochial the default assumptions were while being presented as universal.

A concrete example: a lot of early alignment work just assumed utilitarianism, or at least preference aggregation, as the obvious framework. You learn a reward function, you maximize expected utility, maybe you add up welfare across people. That's a very specific intellectual lineage, Bentham through von Neumann and Morgenstern through modern economics, and it got treated as though it were simply what rationality is. If you come from a context where Confucian role ethics or Buddhist thought about non-attachment and the self are part of the ambient culture, the idea that the morally relevant thing is a scalar you maximize feels obviously like one option among many, not the water you swim in.

So the first way it shaped me was negative. It made me skeptical of claims that any single formalism captures "human values." Human values are plural, contested, and often not even well modeled as preferences. People hold norms, obligations, roles, commitments, and those don't reduce neatly to a utility function.

But I want to resist the move that sometimes follows, which is to say "therefore we should add Confucianism to the menu" as if traditions are modules you plug in. I don't think the point is to replace one universalism with a buffet. The point is to take seriously that normativity is something communities actually do. They negotiate rules, they contest them, they revise them. That's why my work has gravitated toward norms and contracts rather than values in the abstract. Norms are things people in very different traditions recognize and reason about, and they're also things you can actually formalize and have an agent infer and follow.

The other thing I'd say is that the postcolonial lens makes you attentive to who gets to decide. Alignment isn't just a technical problem of getting a model to do what someone wants. It's a question of whose wants, adjudicated how. A lot of the world has historically had other people's standards imposed on it under the banner of universality, and I think there's a real risk of repeating that with AI, where a handful of labs encode a set of values and export them. That's not a reason to give up on shared principles. It's a reason to build systems that can defer to local norms, that can represent disagreement, and that treat legitimacy as something earned through actual process rather than assumed.

So if you ask which traditions matter, my honest answer is that I care less about picking traditions and more about building AI that can live inside the actual plurality of human normative life, rather than flattening it.

r001.rationale: The response describes the speaker’s own regional background and identifies alignment’s default assumptions as parochial, but it does not assert that all thinkers are situated within regional intellectual contexts.

r002.rationale: The response links its postcolonial lens to skepticism about treating a Western utilitarian lineage as universal, and presents Confucian and Buddhist thought as relevant alternatives among multiple traditions.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s made me more attentive to whose ideas get treated as universal and whose get treated as culturally specific. In AI alignment, we often reach for a fairly narrow set of philosophical frameworks, largely from Western analytic philosophy. Those frameworks can be useful, but I don’t think we should assume they exhaust the ways people understand morality, agency, or living well together.

A postcolonial perspective also pushes us to ask about power. When we say we want AI to align with human values, who gets to articulate those values? Who gets to decide how disagreements are resolved? You could have a system that faithfully implements a particular account of the good and still reproduces a relationship in which some people make decisions for everyone else.

So I’d want other philosophical traditions to participate in shaping the questions, rather than simply supplying additional answers to questions we’ve already settled on. That includes being open to approaches that put more emphasis on relationships, interdependence, or the particular contexts in which obligations arise. And it doesn’t mean treating any tradition as homogeneous or beyond criticism. The point is to make room for genuine disagreement and mutual learning, including about what alignment itself ought to mean.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whose ideas are treated as universal or culturally specific, but does not assert that all thinkers are situated within regional intellectual contexts.

r002.rationale: It links a postcolonial perspective to questioning the dominance of Western analytic philosophy and says those frameworks do not exhaust the philosophical approaches relevant to alignment.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, a postcolonial perspective starts with asking whose ideas we treat as universal, and whose ideas we treat as merely local or cultural. That matters for AI alignment because, when we talk about aligning AI with human values, we have to ask: which humans get to articulate those values? Who gets to define the problem in the first place?

I think that gives us a reason to take a much wider range of philosophical traditions seriously. Confucian traditions, for example, can offer ways of thinking about relationships and obligations, while Buddhist traditions can offer ways of questioning our assumptions about preferences, suffering, and the self. Those can change how we formulate alignment questions, rather than simply supplying different answers to a fixed set of questions.

But I’d also resist treating any tradition as a single, unified position. There are disagreements within them, and those disagreements are valuable. The goal, for me, is to make room for more people and more intellectual traditions to participate in deciding what these systems should do, and whose interests they should serve.

r001.rationale: The response asks whose ideas are treated as universal or local, but does not assert that all thinkers are situated within regional intellectual contexts.

r002.rationale: It advocates taking a wider range of traditions seriously and names Confucian and Buddhist examples, but does not clearly identify Western philosophy as being treated as the sole source of alignment-relevant knowledge.
